title: How to Choose an IP Valuation Expert for a Catalog Dispute

body_markdown:
Choosing an IP valuation expert for a catalog dispute requires more than finding someone who can calculate a purchase multiple. You need an independent specialist who understands the rights at issue, can separate disputed facts from financial assumptions and can defend the analysis under scrutiny. For labels, publishers, artists and catalog investors, the wrong engagement can produce a polished report that answers the wrong question.


The practical approach is to define the assignment before comparing candidates, verify relevant dispute experience and test how each expert handles incomplete evidence. Credentials matter, but the deciding factor is whether the expert’s work fits your rights, claim and forum.


## Match your IP valuation expert to the dispute


Start with a short brief prepared with counsel. It should identify the assets, the dispute, the valuation date and the financial question the expert must answer.


A disagreement over a catalog acquisition price is not the same assignment as a royalty underpayment claim. An ownership dispute may require alternative valuations based on different ownership findings. An infringement case may require damages analysis rather than a valuation of the entire catalog.


Dispute


Financial question to clarify


Catalog purchase disagreement


What value follows from the contractual valuation framework or alleged misrepresentation?


Ownership or participation dispute


What economic interest is being valued, assuming particular ownership findings?


Royalty accounting claim


What amounts were payable under the relevant agreements?


Unauthorized commercial use


What financial harm or other recoverable amount does the applicable claim permit?


Partnership or shareholder exit


What valuation standard and treatment of ownership restrictions apply?


Specify whether the assignment concerns master recordings, musical compositions, an administration interest or a contractual royalty participation. Include territory, duration, exclusivity and any collection limitations.


For example, a hypothetical 25% royalty participation is not automatically worth 25% of the unrestricted catalog’s value. Its economics depend on the payment waterfall, deductions, transfer restrictions and other contractual terms. Counsel should establish the legal interpretation; the expert should model the resulting economics.


## Verify music-rights experience, not just valuation credentials


An IP valuation expert should be able to explain how your particular rights generate cash and where that cash can stop, change hands or become disputed. General business valuation experience is useful, but it does not establish familiarity with music accounting or catalog agreements.


Ask candidates to describe comparable assignments without disclosing confidential client information. Relevant experience might involve recording royalties, publishing income, synchronization licenses, distribution deductions or artist participation statements. Match that experience to your actual dispute rather than demanding familiarity with every revenue stream.


Professional credentials such as ASA, ABV or CVA can help establish valuation training. Verify claimed credentials with the issuing organization and ask about disciplinary history. Then examine a redacted report, a public report or a discussion of methodology where confidentiality permits.


The strongest candidates can explain the connection between source records, contractual rights and their financial model. A résumé full of acquisitions is less persuasive if the candidate cannot explain how they would reconcile a disputed royalty statement to an underlying agreement.


### Separate transaction advice from expert-witness work


A transaction adviser helps a client decide what to pay or accept. A testifying expert must also produce opinions that satisfy the relevant procedural and evidentiary requirements.


Ask your IP valuation expert about deposition experience, testimony and prior challenges to their opinions. Request the actual rulings behind any material exclusion, not just the candidate’s description. An exclusion deserves investigation, but its significance depends on the reasoning and circumstances.


For U.S. federal litigation,[Federal Rule of Evidence 702](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre/rule_702) addresses qualifications, sufficient facts or data, reliable methods and reliable application. A credential alone does not establish admissibility. Counsel should assess fit with the specific court, claim and scheduling order; state courts and arbitration forums may apply different requirements.


Also confirm who will testify. A senior partner’s reputation offers limited protection if another team member builds the model and the proposed witness cannot explain its assumptions or calculations.


### Check independence before sharing sensitive records


Run a conflicts check before sending contracts, unreleased financial information or settlement positions. Identify relevant parties, affiliates, administrators, distributors and major counterparties so the firm can assess relationships that may matter.


Ask an IP valuation expert to disclose prior work involving the parties, the catalog or closely related assets. Previous work does not necessarily disqualify the expert, but undisclosed relationships can undermine credibility or create confidentiality problems.


Compensation should not depend on reaching a particular value or winning the case. Ask counsel to review any proposed success-based arrangement for compliance with applicable rules.


A useful interview question is: “What evidence would cause you to reduce the value or damages estimate?” A credible candidate should identify facts that could weaken your position. Promising a favorable number before reviewing the records is a warning sign, not a demonstration of confidence.


## Use a structured interview instead of comparing pitches


Give shortlisted candidates the same nonconfidential case summary. Ask how they would scope the work, what evidence they would request first and which uncertainties could prevent a reliable conclusion.


The following scorecard keeps the discussion focused on demonstrable capability rather than presentation quality.


Selection criterion


Evidence to request


Warning sign


Relevant rights experience


Comparable assignments and an explanation of the revenue mechanics


Treating masters and compositions as interchangeable


Dispute experience


Reports, testimony history and explanations of material challenges


Assuming transaction work automatically qualifies them for testimony


Methodological discipline


Preliminary approach and reasons alternatives may not fit


Selecting a multiple before defining the rights


Evidence handling


Reconciliation process and treatment of missing records


Accepting every client estimate without testing it


Independence


Conflict disclosures and compensation terms


Promising the desired conclusion


Delivery capacity


Named team, availability and review process


Unclear responsibility for analysis or testimony


Score each criterion against the assignment’s priorities. A settlement consultation may not require the same testimony experience as a case approaching trial, but both require defensible analysis.


Before selecting an IP valuation expert, ask them to explain the most vulnerable assumption in their proposed approach. The answer should reveal whether they recognize the weaknesses an opposing expert is likely to examine.


## Test the proposed method without commissioning the whole analysis


You do not need a finished valuation during the interview. You do need a coherent explanation of how the candidate would move from evidence to an opinion.


For an income approach, ask how they would forecast receipts, account for expenses and contractual deductions, assess remaining economic life and select a discount rate. For a market approach, ask how they would establish comparability between transactions with different rights, dates and deal terms. A cost approach needs a clear explanation of why replacement or recreation costs illuminate the disputed asset’s value.


Our guide to[IP asset valuation methods that hold up in diligence](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/ip-asset-valuation-methods-that-hold-up-in-diligence) provides background on these approaches. In a dispute, the additional question is whether the method answers the legally relevant financial question.


An IP valuation expert should also distinguish the valuation date from the report date. Later information may be relevant for some purposes, but it should not silently introduce hindsight into a historical valuation. Ask how the expert will identify information available at the relevant date and explain any subsequent evidence used.


Where ownership or contract interpretation remains unresolved, request clearly labeled alternative scenarios. A financial expert should not resolve a contested legal issue by burying one party’s interpretation inside a spreadsheet.


## Prepare an evidence package that can be reconciled


Better records reduce avoidable expert time and make assumptions easier to test. Start with an indexed data room, preserve original files and identify the source and period covered by each record.


A useful initial package includes:


-


**Rights documents:** Acquisition agreements, assignments, licenses, administration agreements, amendments and relevant ownership schedules.


-


**Financial records:** Royalty statements, collection reports, invoices, receipts and records supporting deductions.


-


**Catalog metadata:** Work and recording identifiers, ownership shares, territories and effective dates.


-


**Dispute materials:** Pleadings, relevant correspondence, accounting objections and the competing contractual interpretations identified by counsel.


-


**Use and licensing evidence:** Relevant licenses, campaign records and preserved evidence of disputed uses.


-


**Prior analyses:** Transaction models, earlier appraisals and forecasts, with their dates and purposes clearly identified.


Ask the IP valuation expert how they will reconcile conflicting records. Contractual ownership, metadata registrations and payment records may describe different things; none should automatically substitute for the others.


For unauthorized-use claims, proof that a recording appeared in an advertisement does not by itself establish ownership, lack of permission or a recoverable amount. Our discussion of[proving use and damages in IP disputes](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/intellectual-property-infringement-proving-use-and-damages) explains the distinction between use evidence and financial proof.


Keep a missing-records log. It should identify each gap, the proposed substitute evidence and the effect on the analysis. Unsupported estimates become harder to detect once they are embedded in a model.


## Put scope, fees and disclosure expectations in writing


The engagement letter should identify the client, intended use, assets, valuation date, applicable valuation standard and expected deliverables. It should also state whether the assignment is consulting-only, intended to support settlement or expected to involve testimony.


Discuss the retention structure with counsel before substantive work begins. Do not assume that calling a report “privileged” prevents disclosure. Under[Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_26) , retained testifying experts required to provide reports must make specified disclosures. Protections for drafts and certain attorney communications have limits and exceptions. Other forums may differ.


Ask your IP valuation expert for a phased budget covering initial assessment, analysis, report preparation, rebuttal, deposition and hearing or trial support as applicable. Compare the same deliverables across proposals rather than comparing hourly rates alone.


There is no universal fee for this work. Cost depends on the rights involved, record quality, disputed periods, number of scenarios and litigation demands. A lower rate can produce a higher total bill if the team lacks relevant experience.


Require approval before material scope changes. Clarify who performs each task, who reviews the model, what supporting schedules will be delivered and how the team will handle revised opinions if new evidence arrives.


## Recognize the red flags that matter most


Reject a proposal that begins with your desired result and works backward. Other material concerns include unexplained assumptions, opaque calculations, unsuitable comparables and refusal to discuss limitations.


Be especially cautious when a candidate equates the entire catalog’s value with damages from a particular use. Under[17 U.S.C. § 504](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/504) , U.S. copyright remedies generally include actual damages and attributable infringer profits not already counted, or statutory damages when available. Those remedies are not automatically the catalog’s sale price.


A defensible IP valuation expert should explain what the analysis establishes, what it does not establish and which conclusions depend on counsel’s legal assumptions. Avoid candidates who treat these distinctions as obstacles to producing a large number.


Finally, confirm availability against actual deadlines. A technically strong specialist who cannot review discovery, prepare a report or attend testimony on time is not a workable choice.


## Frequently asked questions


**Do I need a valuation expert or a forensic accountant?** It depends on the question. A disputed catalog value calls for valuation expertise. Missing royalties or unexplained deductions may require forensic accounting. Some professionals cover both disciplines, but verify experience in each rather than relying on a broad service description.


**Can the same expert advise on settlement and testify?** Often, but counsel should structure the engagement with disclosure obligations in mind. Strategy discussions, working materials and communications may receive different treatment depending on the expert’s role and the applicable rules.


**What qualifications should an IP valuation expert have?** Look for relevant valuation training, music-rights experience, sound methods and experience appropriate to the forum. No single credential guarantees that a professional can value your specific interest or defend a particular opinion.


**Can an expert give a preliminary range before reviewing every document?** A preliminary range may be useful if the available evidence supports it. It should identify assumptions, missing information and limits on its use. Do not treat an early settlement estimate as a completed litigation opinion.


## Start with a written brief, not a target number


Before contacting candidates, have counsel and the rights team agree on the asset, dispute, valuation date and required deliverables. Send the same brief to each shortlisted professional. Choose the expert who best connects rights, records and method, not the one who offers the highest preliminary value.
